newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan, US to announce framework for military pact.
newsitem.headline: Japan, US to announce framework for military pact.

text.p: Japan and the United States are set to announce new security arrangements at the weekend that would give Tokyo its highest military profile in Asia since World War Two, media reports said on Friday.

Under the arrangements, Japan would for the first time conduct minesweeping during an actual conflict, repair U.S. warships and aircraft, join naval blockades of third countries, and fight under a unified military structure if Japan itself is attacked.

The arrangements are part of an interim report after six months of negotiations to review the 1978 "Guidelines for Defence Cooperation" under the 1960 U.S.-Japan Security Treaty, the cornerstone of Washington's defence policy in Asia.
Some details of the interim report were published on Friday by Kyodo news agency and the daily Asahi Shimbun.
It will be unveiled in Honolulu on Saturday after a meeting of Japanese and U.S. defence and foreign affairs officials.
The final report will be issued in November, spelling out details of defence cooperation such as the number of airports to be opened to U.S. warplanes in a future conflict.
The media reports said that despite the planned expansion of its role, Japan has held out against joining in actual combat in an armed conflict in Asia or elsewhere.

Japanese officials were wary of making the role too broad because of the country's pacifist constitution, which bans offensive military actions, and concern that China would regard itself as the target of a newly defined U.S.-Japan military alliance.
Just this week on a visit to Tokyo, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang warned Japan not to enlarge the scope of the security alliance with the United States.

Defence policymakers from Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party are in Beijing this week, possibly to explain to Chinese leaders the outline of the new document before it is formally announced in Honolulu.

When the review began last year, Japan agreed to include discussion of a possible conflict on the Korean peninsula, but refused to discuss measures for possible conflicts between China and Taiwan or over the disputed Spratly Islands in the South China Sea, government sources said.
The old arrangements were mainly based on a possible Soviet invasion of Japan.

According to the media reports, the document says instability and uncertainty in Asia, despite the end of the Cold War, mean that Japan and the United States need an effective means to counter an armed attack on Japan or an armed conflict near Japan.
It says Japan will provide non-weapons logistics support to the U.S. military in the event of a regional conflict but will not provide weapons and ammunition.
The two countries will jointly evacuate civilians, including those from other countries, in a crisis, the reports said. Joint evacuation was not part of earlier arrangements.
They will also study ways to base and repair U.S. warplanes and warships at Japanese ports and airports in a war, again new commitments.
